title: Forward declarations and definitions
recap: A compiler processes declarations in the order it encounters them. A function prototype supplies enough type information to validate a call before the function body appears.
A declaration announces an identifier, while a definition provides its implementation or storage. A called function needs one matching definition in the finished program or linking will fail.
objectives: Write a function prototype before its first use.
Keep declaration and definition signatures consistent.
Distinguish compilation errors from missing-definition linker errors.
Apply the one-definition rule to functions and variables.
warnings: A function prototype ends with a semicolon and has no body.
Changing a parameter or return type can make the declaration describe a different function.
Declaring and calling a function without defining it produces a linker failure.
Fix the first reported diagnostic before investigating later messages.
challenge: In main.cpp, declare roofLoad before main, call it with 12 panels weighing 12 kilograms each, and define it after main. Print the calculated load using the exact output shown.
hints: First, add a prototype for roofLoad above main with the same return type and parameter types as its later definition.

Pseudocode: DECLARE FUNCTION roofLoad(panels: integer, kilogramsPerPanel: integer) RETURNS integer. MAIN: load = roofLoad(12, 12); OUTPUT the calculated-load label, load, and kg suffix; return success. DEFINE FUNCTION roofLoad(panels, kilogramsPerPanel): RETURN panels * kilogramsPerPanel.

Near-C++ structure: int roofLoad(int panels, int kilogramsPerPanel) /* finish as a prototype */ int main() { std::cout << /* label */ << roofLoad(/* required arguments */) << /* suffix and newline */; /* return success */ } int roofLoad(int panels, int kilogramsPerPanel) { return /* product of both parameters */; }
